samples.text:
Today, many children spend most of their free time in organised activities like football clubs, swimming or piano lessons, instead of playing freely with their friends. I think this has more advantages than disadvantages.

The first advantage is that children can learn useful skills. For example, in a music lesson they learn to play an instrument, and in a sports club they learn the rules of a game and how to work in a team. These skills can be helpful for their future and maybe even for their career. Secondly, organised activities are safe, because there is always a teacher or a coach who look after the children. Parents who work all day do not need to worry about where their children is. Also, these activities teach children discipline, because they must come on time and practise regularly.

On the other hand, there are some disadvantages. Children need time to relax and play, but if they have too many activities, they can feel tired and stressed. When children play freely, they use their imagination and create their own games, which is important for their development. In organised activities, the adults decide everything, so children have less chance to be creative. In addition, some activities are expensive, so poor families cannot pay for it.

In conclusion, organised activities have both good and bad sides. They can make children tired and less creative, but they also teach them important skills, discipline and keep them safe. In my opinion, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but parents should not choose too many activity for their children and should leave some time for free play.

samples.text:
Nowadays, many children's free time is filled with structured activities such as sports training, music lessons and language classes, leaving little opportunity for unstructured play. Although these activities offer real benefits, I believe that when they replace free play almost entirely, the disadvantages are greater.

There is no doubt that organised activities can be valuable. They allow children to develop specific talents, whether in football, swimming or playing the violin, under the guidance of qualified instructors. Regular practice also teaches perseverance and time management, and team sports in particular help children learn to cooperate and cope with both winning and losing. For working parents, clubs and lessons provide a safe and supervised environment, which is reassuring when children cannot be left alone at home.

However, free play offers benefits that structured activities cannot provide. When children invent their own games, they have to negotiate rules, solve disagreements and use their imagination without an adult telling them what to do. These experiences develop creativity, independence and social skills that are important throughout life. If every afternoon is scheduled, children lose these opportunities and may become dependent on adults to organise their entertainment. Moreover, a busy timetable of activities can cause stress and tiredness, especially when combined with homework, and some children feel pressured to perform well rather than simply enjoying themselves. There is also a financial aspect, as fees for lessons and equipment can be a heavy burden for many families.

In conclusion, organised activities help children to develop skills and discipline in a safe setting. Nevertheless, as free play is essential for creativity, independence and wellbeing, I believe the drawbacks of filling children's free time with structured activities outweighs the advantages, and a better balance between the two are needed.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both sides extended with relevant support, some generalisation · clear central topic in each paragraph · good collocation (perseverance, heavy burden) · mostly accurate, two agreement slips.

samples.text:
In many families, children's leisure time is now carefully organised around sports clubs, music lessons and tutoring sessions, with unstructured play increasingly squeezed out. While organised activities undoubtedly have value, I would argue that when they come to dominate childhood, their disadvantages outweigh their advantages.

The benefits of structured activities are clear. Expert coaching allows children to acquire skills, from swimming to playing an instrument, that they would be unlikely to master alone, and the discipline of regular practice teaches persistence and the satisfaction of gradual improvement. Team sports and ensembles also foster cooperation and a sense of belonging, while giving children the experience of both success and disappointment in a supportive setting. For parents with demanding jobs, supervised activities offer the additional reassurance that their children are safe and productively occupied.

Free play, however, contributes to development in ways that adult-led activities cannot replicate. When children are left to their own devices, they must invent games, agree on rules and resolve conflicts among themselves, exercising creativity, negotiation and problem-solving in a genuinely independent way. Unstructured time also allows them to explore their own interests rather than those chosen for them, and simply to rest. A childhood filled with back-to-back commitments risks producing young people who are accomplished but anxious, accustomed to constant evaluation and uncomfortable with boredom, which is itself an important stimulus for imagination. The cost of multiple activities can also place considerable strain on family budgets and widen the gap between children from wealthier and poorer households.

In conclusion, organised activities provide valuable skills, discipline and safety, but they cannot substitute for the independence and creativity that free play nurtures. When structured activities largely replace unsupervised play, I believe the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, and families should deliberately protect time for children simply to play.
samples.why: Clear, well-reasoned judgement · ideas fully extended with insightful support · logical sequencing and skilful cohesion · wide, natural vocabulary (left to their own devices, back-to-back commitments) · wide range of error-free structures.
